name: Rosolane Purple
lede: Rosolane Purple is a strong purplish red, the deeper partner to Rosolane Pink in Ridgway's 1912 atlas, from the same unexplained name.

sections.title: The deeper half of a pair
sections.body:
The nearest named colors on file are [[mulberry]] and [[ruber]], at As with that lighter sibling, whether "rosolane" points to rosolic acid, the nineteenth-century coal-tar dye also called aurin, is not stated in Ridgway's own text, so the name's exact origin is left undocumented here [1]. The ISCC-NBS 1955 revision calls this block 255, "strong purplish red" [1][2].

In our library, the hex value is identical to a separately recorded name, [[berry-pink|Berry Pink]], another case of one color carrying two names from two sources [2]. In LCH terms it measures lightness 50, chroma 49, hue 356, close to [[mulberry|Mulberry]] and [[ruber|Ruber]] [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This strong purplish red is nearly absent from our archive: only 3 of 23,781 paintings clear our matching threshold, all from around 1900, as photographed [2]. Its sharpest showing is a 1924 Patrick Henry Bruce still life, where it covers more than a tenth of the canvas [2]. The scarcity before 1900 fits a color this saturated: few historical pigments reached this exact combination of red and purple without fading or shifting [2].

origin.named_after: unexplained in Ridgway's own text; possibly echoes rosolic acid (aurin), unconfirmed

questions.q: Rosolane Purple shares its Ridgway plate and hue number with which lighter color?
True or false: Rosolane Purple and Berry Pink are, by hex value, the exact same color.

openers: Rosolane Purple and Rosolane Pink come from the exact same Ridgway plate and hue — one pale, one strong.
